paras: The attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag and Antone Decker took place on the night of January 26, 1888, when a mob near Santa Ana, Los Angeles County, California, pursued two German prisoners accused of murdering Charles B. Hitchcock and his wife and broke open the Anaheim jail to seize them. Officers had moved the men ahead of the mob, and both were lodged in the Los Angeles county jail the next day. It drew national notice mainly because the first dispatches reported that Anschlag, or both men, had been lynched, a report withdrawn within a day.

The Hitchcocks farmed 20 acres at Garden Grove, about five miles from Santa Ana. Anschlag, a German of 25 who spoke little English, agreed to buy the farm for $8,000. When the couple failed to appear, Anschlag and his hired man, Antone Decker, were arrested, and on January 26 searchers found both bodies buried under straw in a field.

After the discovery a party of lynchers organized at once, but according to the Herald's dispatch Marshal Insley had foreseen the trouble and started the prisoner for Anaheim. A California Associated Press reporter who had been with the lynchers wrote that they rode after the officers, reached Anaheim without overtaking them, and broke open the jail but found no prisoner. The Los Angeles Herald agreed and added that Anschlag had been taken out shortly before and, "it is stated," hidden in a corn-bin.

The Sacramento report told the escape differently: in thick fog the officers turned off at a cross-road, lay out all night, and then took the train to Los Angeles. It credited Constable Farley, spelled Finley in the Herald, with saving the life of Decker, who "as yet stands clear of all evidence of guilt."

A coroner's jury found that the Hitchcocks died from blows of a blunt instrument at the hands of persons unknown and said it believed Fred Anschlag to be one of them. By January 29 the Herald reported that he had confessed and that his confession cleared Decker.

On February 19 a Los Angeles jury convicted Anschlag of first-degree murder after fifteen minutes; a court commission had found him sane. Judge Cheney denied a new trial and sentenced him to hang. He never reached the gallows: an Associated Press dispatch of November 15 reported that he died of strychnine in his cell shortly before his execution date.

The California Associated Press bulletin in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on January 27 said Anschlag had been "summarily lynched" after confessing, along with his "accomplice, Antone Dyker." The Los Angeles Herald that morning carried the same news under the headline "The Assassin Lynched by a Posse of Infuriated Citizens." A national wire ending with Anschlag "lynched before officers could interfere" ran in the Alexandria Gazette and, as "A California Lynching," in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer. A San Francisco special in the Salt Lake Herald and the New North-west went further, saying both men were left hanging to a tree seven miles from Santa Ana.

Corrections came quickly, as the Salt Lake Herald printed a Los Angeles dispatch calling the lynching accounts "incorrect" and a San Francisco dispatch in Nebraska called them "erroneous." The uncorrected story kept circulating, in the Washington Evening Star's "Anschlag, who was lynched," in digest columns into February, and in a Nebraska letter saying the murderer "was lynched, as he ought to have been."

Closer to the scene, the Herald headlined its corrected story "A Disappointed Mob" and later wrote that it was "doubly thankful" the Anaheim threats failed, since an innocent man might have died with the murderer. The Record-Union's editorial ignored the mob and complained of "the slow processes of our laws." No paper gave the race of anyone involved, identifying the accused only as Germans.

The early wire stories said Anschlag, or both men, were hanged; later dispatches from Santa Ana, Los Angeles and San Francisco, the local Herald among them, said the prisoners escaped, and Anschlag's later trial supports that version. The second man appears as Antone Dyker, Anschlag's "supposed partner," in wire reports and as Antonio or Antone Decker, a hired hand, in California papers; no text says whether they are one man.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag and Antone Decker
bases: A mob set out to lynch two jailed suspects in the Hitchcock murders, pursued the officers holding them and broke open the Anaheim jail, but the men had been moved and were not harmed (A4, A5, A10).

A crowd acting without authority hunted the two men as the accused murderers of the Hitchcocks, but the corrected local and wire reports and Anschlag's later trial show no one was killed by the mob (A5, A10, A17, A28); the early reports of a hanging were retracted (A12, A24).

The local Herald, the California AP reporter who followed the mob, and Los Angeles and San Francisco dispatches agree that a mob pursued the prisoners and broke into the Anaheim jail without finding them (A5, A10, A12, A17); the first wire reports of a completed lynching were withdrawn by the same services and contradicted by Anschlag's trial (A28, A29).

accounts.gist: Anschlag, and in some versions Dyker too, was overtaken by a lynching party and hanged before officers could interfere.

accounts.label: Corrected report (reporter with the mob; local Herald)
accounts.gist: The mob pursued the officers and broke into the Anaheim jail but found no prisoner; the officers evaded it in fog or hid the men, then took them to the Los Angeles jail.

accounts.label: Los Angeles and San Francisco corrections
accounts.gist: The lynching accounts were incorrect or erroneous; the men were hidden in Anaheim overnight and jailed.

accounts.label: Trial report
accounts.gist: Anschlag and another man, later shown to have had nothing to do with the crime, narrowly escaped lynching.

framing.detail: National papers ran the wire's lynching as fact under heads such as 'A CALIFORNIA LYNCHING' and 'Speedy Punishment of his Murderer', some later adding a correction.

The Los Angeles Herald first headlined 'The Assassin Lynched by a Posse of Infuriated Citizens', then 'A DISAPPOINTED MOB', and editorially was 'doubly thankful' the threats failed because an innocent man might have died.
A Nebraska neighborhood letter said the murderer 'was lynched, as he ought to have been'.
The Sacramento Record-Union editorial ignored the mob and attacked 'the slow processes of our laws'.
